Introducing advanced tool use on the Claude Developer Platform \ Anthropic (https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/advanced-tool-use)
citeturn2103view0 [wordlim: 200] Crawled: today; Content type: text/html; Source: open({"ref_id":"https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/advanced-tool-use","lineno":182}); Total lines: 490
L129: #### Example: Budget compliance check
L130: 
L131: Consider a common business task: "Which team members exceeded their Q3 travel budget?"
L132: 
L133: You have three tools available:
L134: 
L135:   * `get_team_members(department)` - Returns team member list with IDs and levels
L136:   * `get_expenses(user_id, quarter)` - Returns expense line items for a user
L137:   * `get_budget_by_level(level)` - Returns budget limits for an employee level
L138: 
L139: Traditional approach:
L140:   * Fetch team members → 20 people
L141:   * For each person, fetch their Q3 expenses → 20 tool calls, each returning 50-100 line items (flights, hotels, meals, receipts)
L142:   * Fetch budget limits by employee level
L143:   * All of this enters Claude's context: 2,000+ expense line items (50 KB+)
L144:   * Claude manually sums each person's expenses, looks up their budget, compares expenses against budget limits
L145:   * More round-trips to the model, significant context consumption
L146: 
L147: With Programmatic Tool Calling:
L148: Instead of each tool result returning to Claude, Claude writes a Python script that orchestrates the entire workflow. The script runs in the Code Execution tool (a sandboxed environment), pausing when it needs results from your tools. When you return tool results via the API, they're processed by the script rather than consumed by the model. The script continues executing, and Claude only sees the final output.
L149: cite11†Image: Programmatic tool calling flow Programmatic Tool Calling enables Claude to orchestrate tools through code rather than through individual API round-trips, allowing for parallel tool execution.
L150: Here's what Claude's orchestration code looks like for the budget compliance task:
L151: 
L152:     `team = await get_team_members("engineering")
L153: 
L154:     # Fetch budgets for each unique level
L155:     levels = list(set(m["level"] for m in team))
L156:     budget_results = await asyncio.gather(*[
L157:         get_budget_by_level(level) for level in levels
L158:     ])
L159: 
L160:     # Create a lookup dictionary: {"junior": budget1, "senior": budget2, ...}
L161:     budgets = {level: budget for level, budget in zip(levels, budget_results)}
L162:     # Fetch all expenses in parallel
L163:     expenses = await asyncio.gather(*[
L164:         get_expenses(m["id"], "Q3") for m in team
L165:     ])
L166: 
L167:     # Find employees who exceeded their travel budget
L168:     exceeded = []
L169:     for member, exp in zip(team, expenses):
L170:         budget = budgets[member["level"]]
L171:         total = sum(e["amount"] for e in exp)
L172:         if total > budget["travel_limit"]:
L173:             exceeded.append({
L174:                 "name": member["name"],
L175:                 "spent": total,
L176:                 "limit": budget["travel_limit"]
L177:             })
L178: 
L179:     print(json.dumps(exceeded))`
L180: Copy
L181: 
L182: Claude's context receives only the final result: the two to three people who exceeded their budget. The 2,000+ line items, the intermediate sums, and the budget lookups do not affect Claude’s context, reducing consumption from 200KB of raw expense data to just 1KB of results.
L183: 
L184: The efficiency gains are substantial:
L185:   * Token savings: By keeping intermediate results out of Claude's context, PTC dramatically reduces token consumption. Average usage dropped from 43,588 to 27,297 tokens, a 37% reduction on complex research tasks.
L186:   * Reduced latency: Each API round-trip requires model inference (hundreds of milliseconds to seconds). When Claude orchestrates 20+ tool calls in a single code block, you eliminate 19+ inference passes. The API handles tool execution without returning to the model each time.
L187:   * Improved accuracy: By writing explicit orchestration logic, Claude makes fewer errors than when juggling multiple tool results in natural language. Internal knowledge retrieval improved from 25.6% to 28.5%; cite12†GIA benchmarks†arxiv.org from 46.5% to 51.2%.
L188: Production workflows involve messy data, conditional logic, and operations that need to scale. Programmatic Tool Calling lets Claude handle that complexity programmatically while keeping its focus on actionable results rather than raw data processing.
L189: ### How Programmatic Tool Calling works
L190: #### 1. Mark tools as callable from code
L191: Add code_execution to tools, and set allowed_callers to opt-in tools for programmatic execution:
L192: 
L193:     `{
L194:       "tools": [
L195:         {
L196:           "type": "code_execution_20250825",
L197:           "name": "code_execution"
L198:         },
L199:         {
L200:           "name": "get_team_members",
L201:           "description": "Get all members of a department...",
L202:           "input_schema": {...},
L203:           "allowed_callers": ["code_execution_20250825"] # opt-in to programmatic tool calling
L204:         },
L205:         {
L206:           "name": "get_expenses",
L207:      	...
L208:         },
L209:         {
L210:           "name": "get_budget_by_level",
L211:     	...
L212:         }
L213:       ]
L214:     }`
L215: Copy
L216: 
L217: The API converts these tool definitions into Python functions that Claude can call.
L218: #### 2. Claude writes orchestration code
L219: 
L220: Instead of requesting tools one at a time, Claude generates Python code:
L221: 
L222:     `{
L223:       "type": "server_tool_use",
L224:       "id": "srvtoolu_abc",
L225:       "name": "code_execution",
L226:       "input": {
L227:         "code": "team = get_team_members('engineering')\n..." # the code example above
L228:       }
L229:     }`
L230: 
L231: Copy
L232: #### 3. Tools execute without hitting Claude's context
L233: 
L234: When the code calls get_expenses(), you receive a tool request with a caller field:
L235: 
L236:     `{
L237:       "type": "tool_use",
L238:       "id": "toolu_xyz",
L239:       "name": "get_expenses",
L240:       "input": {"user_id": "emp_123", "quarter": "Q3"},
L241:       "caller": {
L242:         "type": "code_execution_20250825",
L243:         "tool_id": "srvtoolu_abc"
L244:       }
L245:     }`
L246: 
L247: Copy
L248: You provide the result, which is processed in the Code Execution environment rather than Claude's context. This request-response cycle repeats for each tool call in the code.
L249: #### 4. Only final output enters context
L250: 
L251: When the code finishes running, only the results of the code are returned to Claude:
L252: 
L253:     `{
L254:       "type": "code_execution_tool_result",
L255:       "tool_use_id": "srvtoolu_abc",
L256:       "content": {
L257:         "stdout": "[{\"name\": \"Alice\", \"spent\": 12500, \"limit\": 10000}...]"
L258:       }
L259:     }`
L260: 
L261: Copy
L262: 
L263: This is all Claude sees, not the 2000+ expense line items processed along the way.
L264: ### When to use Programmatic Tool Calling
L265: 
L266: Programmatic Tool Calling adds a code execution step to your workflow. This extra overhead pays off when the token savings, latency improvements, and accuracy gains are substantial.
L267: 
L268: Most beneficial when:
L269:   * Processing large datasets where you only need aggregates or summaries
L270:   * Running multi-step workflows with three or more dependent tool calls
L271:   * Filtering, sorting, or transforming tool results before Claude sees them
L272:   * Handling tasks where intermediate data shouldn't influence Claude's reasoning
L273:   * Running parallel operations across many items (checking 50 endpoints, for example)
L274: 
L275: Less beneficial when:
L276:   * Making simple single-tool invocations
L277:   * Working on tasks where Claude should see and reason about all intermediate results
L278:   * Running quick lookups with small responses
L279: ## Tool Use Examples
L280: ### The challenge
L281: 
L282: JSON Schema excels at defining structure–types, required fields, allowed enums–but it can't express usage patterns: when to include optional parameters, which combinations make sense, or what conventions your API expects.
L283: Consider a support ticket API:
L284: 
L285:     `{
L286:       "name": "create_ticket",
L287:       "input_schema": {
L288:         "properties": {
L289:           "title": {"type": "string"},
L290:           "priority": {"enum": ["low", "medium", "high", "critical"]},
L291:           "labels": {"type": "array", "items": {"type": "string"}},
L292:           "reporter": {
L293:             "type": "object",
L294:             "properties": {
L295:               "id": {"type": "string"},
L296:               "name": {"type": "string"},
L297:               "contact": {
L298:                 "type": "object",
L299:                 "properties": {
L300:                   "email": {"type": "string"},
L301:                   "phone": {"type": "string"}
L302:                 }
L303:               }
L304:             }
L305:           },
L306:           "due_date": {"type": "string"},
L307:           "escalation": {
L308:             "type": "object",
L309:             "properties": {
L310:               "level": {"type": "integer"},
L311:               "notify_manager": {"type": "boolean"},
L312:               "sla_hours": {"type": "integer"}
L313:             }
L314:           }
L315:         },
L316:         "required": ["title"]
L317:       }
L318:     }`
L319: Copy
L320: 
L321: The schema defines what's valid, but leaves critical questions unanswered:
L322: 
L323:   * Format ambiguity: Should `due_date` use "2024-11-06", "Nov 6, 2024", or "2024-11-06T00:00:00Z"?
L324:   * ID conventions: Is `reporter.id` a UUID, "USR-12345", or just "12345"?

MicroMoE: Fine-grained Load Balancing for Mixture-of-Experts with Token Scheduling (https://arxiv.org/html/2511.16947v1)
citeturn2103view1 [wordlim: 200] Crawled: yesterday; Content type: text/html; Source: open({"ref_id":"https://arxiv.org/html/2511.16947v1","lineno":315}); Total lines: 601
L307: Relationship between token scheduling and adaptive replacement. The adaptive replacement mechanism complements the token scheduling in §cite15†5 by addressing different levels of load balancing. Token scheduling performs transient, fine-grained load balancing through per-micro-batch token arrangement, while adaptive replacement handles long-term, coarse-grained load imbalances through periodic expert arrangement.
L308: Specifically, for moderately imbalanced workloads, token scheduling effectively maintains optimal balance with static, symmetric placements (as shown in §cite28†7.3 ). For highly skewed workloads, MicroMoE adopts asymmetric placements to mitigate coarse-grained imbalances before using token scheduling for fine-grained optimization.
L309: Since asymmetric placements require real-time expert loads, MicroMoE adopts adaptive replacement to monitor expert load distributions and adjust placements when significant distributional shifts are detected.
L310: Implementation of adaptive replacement. We implement the adaptive replacement mechanism in MicroMoE using the placement manager (according to Figure cite101†4 ). (1) During model initialization, the placement manager initializes the model states of all devices using the symmetric placement strategy, providing conservative and general load balancing capabilities. (2) During training, the placement manager monitors expert load information within each micro-batch in the background.
L311: (3) For every few iterations, the placement manager predicts future load distributions using historical data with time series analysis techniques, such as moving averages (cite111†Cong et al., 2024 ). Then, it evaluates the performance of current placements on future distributions using Equation cite109†3 . If the future performance drops below a specific threshold, the placement manager generates new optimal asymmetric placements and re-initializes global model states accordingly.
L312: Difference between MicroMoE’s adaptive replacement and expert scheduling solutions. The system implementation of MicroMoE’s adaptive replacement is similar to existing expert scheduling solutions, such as FlexMoE (cite78†Nie et al., 2023 ) and SmartMoE (cite77†Zhai et al., 2023 ). Nevertheless, their design goals and algorithms are fundamentally different:
L313: Design goals: In FlexMoE, changing expert placement is the only means for load balancing. However, in MicroMoE, the primary weapon is token scheduling, while adaptive replacement is a further optimization to token scheduling. Even with static placement, MicroMoE can still achieve good load balancing performance at the micro-batch granularity.
L314: Algorithms: The different design goals of FlexMoE and MicroMoE lead to different placement algorithms. In FlexMoE, all replicas of an expert have identical loads, i.e., the replica load is simply calculated as the expert load divided by the replica count. In contrast, the replica loads in MicroMoE are determined by the LPP cite102†1 . Therefore, MicroMoE requires the graph theory in §cite21†6.1 to guide the placement strategy.
L315: ## 7. Evaluation
L316: ### 7.1. Experimental Setup
L317: 
L318: Testbed. Our testbed consists of 4 nodes, each equipped with 8 NVIDIA H100 80GB SXM GPUs connected via 900 GBps NVLink. Nodes are interconnected using two 400 Gbps Infiniband NICs per node.
L319: Models. We use GPT (cite112†Brown et al., 2020 ) and Mixtral (cite113†Jiang et al., 2024 ) models for evaluation. We use GPT 32$\times$1.3B to represent an MoE model converted from a 1.3B dense GPT model with 32 experts. We pretrain these models with the Wikipedia dataset (cite114†Foundation, 2025 ). A detailed list of model hyperparameters is provided in Appendix cite44†C.1 .
L320: 
L321: Baselines. We compare MicroMoE with four baseline systems.
L322: 
L323:   * •
L324: Megatron-LM (cite83†Shoeybi et al., 2020 ) is a popular distributed training framework for large language models (LLMs). It supports various parallelism strategies, as well as state-of-the-art optimizations (cite115†Chen et al., 2016 ).
L325: 
L326:   * •
L327: 
L328: SmartMoE (cite77†Zhai et al., 2023 ) balances GPU loads by adjusting the expert placement within EP groups.
L329: 
L330:   * •
L331: FlexMoE (cite78†Nie et al., 2023 ) achieves load balancing by dynamically adjusting replica counts based on expert loads. FlexMoE places expert replicas across the entire DP group, similar to MicroMoE’s asymmetric placement (§cite23†6.3 ).
L332: 
L333:   * •
L334: DeepSpeed (cite84†Rasley et al., 2020 ) is a high-performance distributed framework for both LLM training and inference. We enable ZeRO-1 (cite88†Rajbhandari et al., 2020 ) optimization in DeepSpeed (currently, ZeRO-2 does not support PP, and Tutel (cite105†Hwang et al., 2023 ) does not support top-K>1).
L335: 
L336: We compare two variants of MicroMoE: “MicroMoE (w/o AR)” uses static, symmetric placement (§cite22†6.2 ), while “MicroMoE” uses adaptive, asymmetric placement (§cite23†6.3 -cite24†6.4 ).
L337: Figure 6. End-to-end speedup of different systems compared with Megatron-LM.
L338: Implementation. We implement MicroMoE upon Megatron-LM (cite83†Shoeybi et al., 2020 ). MicroMoE provides a model wrapper similar to Pytorch’s Distributed Data Parallel (DDP) (cite116†Li et al., 2020 ), enabling users to benefit from MicroEP’s fine-grained load balancing capabilities within their training jobs. We modify Megatron-LM, including its MoELayer and DDP with Python, and implement the token scheduling algorithm in MicroEP with C++.
L339: For fair comparison, we also implement SmartMoE and FlexMoE in Megatron-LM, as SmartMoE’s repository is outdated (last commit in 2023) (cite77†Zhai et al., 2023 ), and FlexMoE is not open-sourced (cite78†Nie et al., 2023 ).
L340: Parallelization configurations. Due to the limited inter-node network bandwidth in our testbed, we only employ PP for inter-node parallelism. Specifically, we set the PP degree to the number of nodes used, and the DP degree to 8. We set the EP degree to 4, resulting in 2 EP groups per DP group. We set the parameter $d$ in MicroEP to 2, resulting in a single MicroEP group per DP group. We disable TP due to its high communication overhead.
L341: Other configurations. We use a small auxiliary loss (listed in the appendix) to prevent extreme load imbalance from degrading model accuracy. We enable the distributed optimizers in Megatron-LM, which resembles DeepSpeed’s ZeRO-1 (cite88†Rajbhandari et al., 2020 ). We disable the token dropping mechanism introduced by GShard (cite66†Lepikhin et al., 2020 ). We use BF16 precision.
L342: ### 7.2. End-to-end Performance
L343: Figure cite117†6 shows the end-to-end performance of all systems, varying models and number of GPUs. DeepSpeed exhibits poor performance with 16 or 32 experts. This is because DeepSpeed always adopts a padding mechanism, padding the load of each expert to the maximum expert load (cite66†Lepikhin et al., 2020 ). This mechanism wastes significant time and memory when expert loads are highly imbalanced.
L344: With as few as 8 experts, the inefficiency of padding becomes less significant, allowing DeepSpeed to outperform Megatron-LM due to its system-level optimizations.
L345: Comparing SmartMoE and MicroMoE (w/o AR), where experts have uniform replica counts, MicroMoE (w/o AR) exhibits superior performance, thanks to MicroEP’s fine-grained token scheduling. While SmartMoE attempts to optimize performance by changing expert placement for load balancing among GPUs, it sometimes performs worse than vanilla Megatron-LM. This is because SmartMoE optimizes expert placement based on long-term expert load distributions.
L346: However, expert loads are highly dynamic during training, and SmartMoE’s long-term optimal placement may be sub-optimal for individual micro-batches.
L347: Comparing FlexMoE and MicroMoE (with AR), where experts have varied replica counts, MicroMoE exhibits superior performance, thanks to MicroEP. Compared with Megatron-LM, MicroMoE improves the end-to-end throughput by up to 47.6%, with an average improvement of 36.9%. The average performance improvement of MicroMoE surpasses FlexMoE, the second-best system, by 13.9%.
L348: 
L349: Figure 7. Max GPU load normalized by average GPU load, varying skewness of expert loads. DP_degree=8, num_experts=32.
L350: ### 7.3. Load Balancing Capability
L351: 
L352: We evaluate the load balancing capabilities of SmartMoE, FlexMoE, and MicroMoE with skewed expert loads. We generate expert loads following a Zipfian distribution with skewness $s$, where the probability of a token being assigned to the $i$-th most loaded expert is proportional to $i^{-s}$.
L353: Figure cite118†7 shows the load balancing performance of different systems across varied skewness $s$. SmartMoE’s maximum GPU load increases as load skewness increases. While FlexMoE maintains relatively balanced GPU loads by adjusting expert replica counts, it falls short of achieving optimal load balance due to its lack of fine-grained dynamicity. MicroMoE (random) represents MicroMoE with pure random placement, which performs slightly worse than MicroMoE (w/o AR) with symmetric placement.

Masked-and-Reordered Self-Supervision for Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards (https://arxiv.org/html/2511.17473v1)
citeturn2103view2 [wordlim: 200] Crawled: today; Content type: text/html; Source: open({"ref_id":"https://arxiv.org/html/2511.17473v1","lineno":190}); Total lines: 338
L177: To accommodate diverse reasoning styles, we construct our training corpus from two data sources: DeepTheorem(cite58†Zhang et al., 2025 ) primarily contains theorem-proving problems, while DeepMath (cite59†He et al., 2025 ) focuses on computational reasoning tasks. We sample 10k problems equally from both datasets.
L178: Since the reasoning traces in DeepMath are generated by DeepSeek models and contain multiple internal verification steps that may lead to information leakage within trajectories, we refine all DeepMath samples using GPT-o3-mini to ensure clean, step-by-step reasoning without redundant self-verification.
L179: As identifying key theorems, formulas, and reasoning steps for masking or reordering is non-trivial, we employ DeepSeek-R1-0528 to process the refined reasoning trajectories and generate task-specific annotations: masked positions for the Masked-Then-Fill task and step boundaries for the Step Reordering task (prompt templates in Appendix cite34†A ). To avoid trivial masking tasks, we retain only samples with at least 7 masked positions.
L180: From the filtered pool, we select 10k samples for each of the two tasks (Masked-Then-Fill and Step Reordering), randomly sampling 20k instances for Stage I training and 6k for validation. For Stage II fine-tuning, we select 5k computational reasoning samples from the Stage I training data as the training set, with 1.5k held out for validation, ensuring that Stage II focuses on verifiable computational problems with deterministic answers.
L181: ##### Model Configuration
L182: We conduct experiments on Qwen2.5-3B-Base(cite60†Qwen et al., 2025 ) and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B(cite41†Guo et al., 2025 ). We employ the GRPO objective for reinforcement learning. All experiments are conducted within the verl framework (cite61†Sheng et al., 2025 ) on a single node with 8 NVIDIA A100 (80 GB) or A800 (80 GB) GPUs. To optimize GPU memory usage, several parameters differ slightly between Qwen-3B and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5.
L183: Detailed experimental hyperparameters can be found in the Appendix cite37†B .
L184: ##### Evaluation Setup
L185: 
L186: We evaluate reasoning performance on four challenging mathematical benchmarks: AIME 2024, AIME 2025, AMC 2023 cite62†Li et al., 2024 , and MATH500 cite63†Hendrycks et al., 2021 . We report the unbiased estimator of Pass@$k$ cite64†Chen et al. (2021) , defined as
L187: 
L188:  | $$\text{Pass@}k=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}\left[1-\frac{\binom{n-c}{k}}{\binom{n}{k}}\right],$$  |  | (7)
L189: where $n$ is the number of generated solutions per problem, $c$ is the number of correct solutions, and $k\in\{1,5,8\}$ denotes the number of attempts allowed. We set $n=64$ for all evaluations. During inference, we use nucleus sampling with temperature 0.6, top-$p$ 0.95, and a maximum generation length of 4096 tokens. Answers are verified programmatically through symbolic computation using MathRuler cite65†hiyouga (2025) and text matching.

L210: Table cite66†1 presents the main experimental results comparing our MR-RLVR method against the GRPO baseline across four mathematical reasoning benchmarks. Overall, MR-RLVR demonstrates consistent performance improvements over GRPO, particularly in challenging scenarios where baseline performance is relatively low. On the Qwen2.5-3B model, we observe substantial gains on AIME 2025, with Pass@1, Pass@5, and Pass@8 achieving relative improvements of 35.98%, 22.44%, and 16.11%, respectively.
L211: Similar trends are evident in AIME24 Pass@1 (+12.04%) and across all metrics on AMC23 (+5.29% to +12.98%).
L212: Interestingly, the performance gains exhibit interesting patterns across different model architectures and task difficulties. In terms of average improvement magnitude, MR-RLVR yields significantly larger gains on Qwen2.5-3B (average 8.29%) compared to DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B (average 4.47%).
L213: This discrepancy may be attributed to the fact that the former has only undergone basic pretraining without complex post-training procedures, thus offering greater room for optimization through verification enhancement. Another notable observation is that both models show relatively limited improvements on MATH500 (0.13%-4.06%).
L214: This is not only because the baseline performance is already high (Pass@1>78%), but more importantly, the problems in MATH500 are relatively simple and the models have largely mastered their solution patterns, resulting in minimal marginal gains from multi-round verification. In contrast, our method demonstrates much stronger value on competition-level problems such as AIME and AMC.
L215: We also observe minor performance degradation on AIME24 Pass@5/Pass@8 for Qwen2.5-3B, which we attribute to the inherent variance in the sampling process with n=64 samples.
L216: These results validate the effectiveness of our MR-RLVR framework in improving mathematical reasoning capabilities. The consistent gains on challenging benchmarks (AIME24, AIME25, AMC23) demonstrate that MR-RLVR successfully enhances the model’s ability to generate and verify correct solutions, particularly in scenarios where baseline performance leaves substantial room for improvement.
L217: Meanwhile, the more modest improvements on relatively simple tasks like MATH500 indicate that our method provides maximum value when applied to high-difficulty problems at the boundary of model competence, which aligns well with the design principle of MR-RLVR, to tackle complex reasoning tasks not yet fully mastered by the model through iterative refinement.
